title: The Ledger's Door
passages:
Ash shifted under Tomas's palm. He did not put it in the stove. He did not put it in the flour crock, where it sank without sound. Maren watched him, then Ákos. "You want to write her name again," she said. It was not a question. Ákos's throat worked. He had no voice for it, only the hollow where Elise had been. He nodded. Ilka went to the door and looked out at the rain, her shoulders straight.

Ákos looked at the black stove, the cooling hearthstone, the dark sixth tag. "Then the tag is wrong," he said. "The ledger wrote Kornél. The doll burned. The name went back to him." Maren did not answer. Tomas wiped the table edge with his good hand, leaving a pale smear. Sára opened the ledger again. Her hand hovered over the page, and the pen made a small sound against the paper. Her voice came back in pieces, shaped words without sound, asking if anyone remembered the drowned woman's name before the flood.

No one did. Tomas said the marsh would keep it. Ilka watched the rain streak the shutters. Ákos put his hand on the table edge and felt Maren watching him. He did not ask Maren to sew the face again. He did not ask Sára for the pen. He only said, very quietly, that he would write the name himself.

Ákos took the pen out of Sára's fingers. She let it go without resistance, and the small sound of the nib on paper filled the room. He wrote *Elise* slowly, in his own letters, and watched them change under his hand into Sára's cramped script, wet and slanted, as though someone wrote alongside him. When the last letter closed, a cold pressed behind his eyes and took something with it: the smell of river mud on a pair of boots, a laugh he could hear but not place. The sixth tag stayed dark. The hearthstone did not warm.

"That's the price," Maren said. "The ledger took the echo. It won't give the fragment back. That's gone to the one who carried her."

Tomas turned his empty sleeve over in his fingers. "So we've marked the page twice and got nothing."

"We got the name written," Ákos said. His voice came out thin but steady. "In the book. Twice."

Sára looked at him sharply. Beneath the entry for Elise, her cramped hand had begun again, without pen: *Vass, Ákos. Debt carried. Fragment held by another.* Ákos read it twice. "It says I'm owed," he said. "It doesn't say who pays."

"No," Maren said. "It won't."

Ilka came back from the door and took her tongs off the table, hung them on their nail. "The stove is out. The stone will be cold by morning. A hearthstone with no lit tag —" She stopped, and did not finish, and no one made her.

Ákos pulled his notebook from his coat and laid it beside the ledger. He opened it to the last page, where his losses were listed in his own bad hand: a dog, a summer, Elise. Then he wrote her name again — not in the ledger, in his own book, with his own pen. Nothing changed. The letters stayed his, crooked and small. The hollow in him rang like a struck cup, but the ink was only ink.

"That's mine," he said. "Whatever the ledger does, this book does it differently. It doesn't take."

Maren leaned over the page. "It will take something," she said. "Everything does, boy. It just hasn't told you the price yet."

"Then I'll find out." Ákos closed the notebook and put it back inside his coat. Through the shutter slats the causeway lay grey and empty where Kornél had gone. "He has what I lost. I want to know what he means to do with it."

Tomas lifted his coat off the peg. "The hut's two bends up. If we walk now we'll catch him before the bend."

Sára closed the ledger with one flat palm, and her shaped words came without sound: *Go, then. I'll keep the page.*
